title: TCP, UDP & Latency
summary: How data actually travels: protocols, TCP's reliable connections and handshake, fast but unreliable UDP, and latency.

blocks.text: Two harbors can only trade if they agree on the paperwork: which form to use, what goes in each box, what a stamp means. A harbor that fills in the form its own way just gets its parcels sent back. That shared rulebook is a **protocol**.

A **protocol** is a set of rules for how data is exchanged between computers. Two devices can only talk if they agree on the **format** of the data they send. The rest of this subject is a tour of the protocols the Internet runs on.

For valuable cargo the harbor uses **registered freight** (TCP). Both sides agree to the shipment first, every crate is numbered, and the receiver signs for each one, so nothing goes missing and everything is unpacked in order. A new route starts with small loads and grows them while the canal can take more.
**TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) lets two computers **connect** and send each other streams of data. It is the careful option.

items: It **guarantees delivery**: data and packets arrive, error-free, in the **same order** they were sent.
It uses **congestion control**: a connection starts by sending a little, then sends more until it reaches what the computers and network can handle.

blocks.text: Use TCP when every byte must arrive, error-free and in order.

Before registered freight moves, the two harbors trade three radio calls. "Ready to sync?" (SYN). "Synced, are you?" (SYN-ACK). "Acknowledged." (ACK). Only then do crates move. Hanging up is politer still: each side says "finished" (FIN) and gets an "okay" (ACK), so one side can keep sending after the other is done.
Before any data moves, TCP sets up the connection with three messages, so both sides can agree on its settings:

items: 1. **SYN** (synchronize): the initiator, usually the browser, asks the server to connect.
3. **ACK** (acknowledge): the initiator confirms. The connection is now open.

blocks.text: Closing uses a **four-way handshake**: each side sends its own **FIN** (finish) and gets an **ACK** back. In between, the connection is **half-closed**: one side is done, but the other can still send.
Order when opening a secure web page: **DNS lookup**, then the **TCP handshake**, then the **TLS handshake**.

For live harbor traffic reports, nobody wants registered freight. The harbor radio just **broadcasts** each update (UDP). No call to set it up, no signatures, no resends. A missed report is simply skipped, because the next one is already on the way, and waiting for an old one would be worse than useless.
**UDP** (User Datagram Protocol) is for when **speed and efficiency matter more than reliability**. There is no connection to set up: no handshake. It just sends.

items: It has **port numbers** (to reach the right program) and **checksums** (to spot damaged data), and very little else.
There is **no guarantee** of delivery, of order, or against duplicates.
Time-sensitive apps use it because **dropping a packet beats waiting** for a resend.
Apps that need error correction can use TCP instead, or do the checking themselves.

blocks.text: **Latency** is how long a parcel takes from the dock to its door. Low latency means the parcel is there almost at once; high latency means everyone waits. Delay can also build up at the packing table, when goods are repacked into a new format (codec latency), but on the routes between harbors it is the crossing time that counts (network latency).
**Latency** is the time it takes for requested data to reach its destination. **Low latency is good** (little delay); **high latency is bad**.
**Network latency** usually means the time for a packet to travel from source to destination.

To time a route, the harbor sends a parcel and waits for the signed receipt to come back. Out plus back is the **round trip** (RTT). The harbor's test signal (`ping`) does this a few times and reports the shortest, average and longest trips.
**Round-trip time (RTT)** is the time for a packet to reach its destination **plus** the time for the acknowledgment to come back. The `ping` command measures it:
ping <hostname>
`ping` sends a few packets, prints the time for each, then a summary line: `round-trip min/avg/max/stddev`. The **avg** value is the average RTT, in milliseconds.

sections.heading: Where this shows up in Kubernetes

blocks.text: Every harbor phone number (Service) is set up for a kind of freight. Registered freight (TCP) is the default and works for every kind of number. Radio broadcasts (UDP) work for most, but on the public entrance the city builds (`LoadBalancer`), the city must support it. A third kind, SCTP, needs road builders (network plugins) that support it.
Each port on a Kubernetes **Service** has a `protocol`. There are three valid values:

items: `TCP`: **the default**, and works for every kind of Service.
`UDP`: works for most Services. For `type: LoadBalancer`, it depends on your cloud provider supporting it.
`SCTP`: needs a network plugin that supports it. For `LoadBalancer` it depends on the cloud provider (most don't), and it isn't supported on Windows nodes.

blocks.text: HTTP, HTTPS and TLS are special cases that all typically run over TCP.

flashcards.back: A system of rules defining how data is exchanged between computers, including the data's format.
Delivery of data and packets, error-free, in the same order they were sent.
Connections start sending small amounts, then increase to what the computers and network can support.

flashcards.front: Name the three messages of the TCP handshake, in order.
How is a TCP connection closed?
flashcards.back: A four-way handshake: each side sends a FIN and receives an ACK, independently.

flashcards.front: When does the TCP handshake happen relative to DNS and TLS?
flashcards.back: After the DNS lookup and before the TLS handshake.
No. It is connectionless, with no handshaking dialogues.
Port numbers and checksums. No guarantee of delivery, ordering or duplicate protection.

flashcards.front: Why do time-sensitive apps use UDP?
flashcards.back: Dropping a packet is better than waiting for a delayed retransmission.
The time it takes for requested data to reach its destination. Low is good, high is bad.
Time for a packet to reach its destination plus time for the acknowledgment to come back. Measured with `ping`.
How much information can pass through a connection in a given time, usually in bits per second (Mbps, Gbps).

flashcards.front: What does HTTP/3 use instead of TCP?
flashcards.back: QUIC, a multiplexed transport protocol built on UDP.

flashcards.front: Default protocol for a Kubernetes Service port?
flashcards.back: TCP. UDP and SCTP are the other valid values.

questions.stem: Why do two computers need a shared protocol?

options.text: They must agree on the format of the data they exchange
options.explanation: A protocol is that agreed set of rules.
Addressing is one protocol's job, not why protocols exist.
Encryption is a feature of some protocols such as TLS.

options.text: To use the same operating system
options.explanation: Protocols let different systems talk.

questions.stem: A file download must arrive complete and in the right order. Which transport fits?

options.explanation: TCP guarantees delivery, in order and error-free.
UDP gives no guarantee of delivery or order.
IP addresses and routes packets; it isn't the reliable transport layer.
DNS maps names to addresses.

questions.stem: What does TCP congestion control do when a connection starts?

options.text: Sends small amounts first, then grows to what the network can handle
options.explanation: That's how TCP finds the available capacity.

options.text: Sends as fast as possible, then backs off
options.explanation: It starts small rather than at full speed.

options.text: Waits for the server's bandwidth report
options.explanation: There's no such report; it ramps up gradually.

options.text: Drops late packets to avoid delay
options.explanation: That's UDP's trade-off, not TCP's.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the TCP three-way handshake?

options.explanation: Initiator sends SYN, server replies SYN-ACK, initiator confirms with ACK.
FIN is for closing a connection.
The initiator starts with SYN.
That mixes closing and opening messages.

questions.stem: A browser opens an HTTPS page on a site it has never visited. Which happens first?

options.explanation: The handshake happens after the DNS lookup and before the TLS handshake.
It needs the IP address from the DNS lookup first.
TLS comes after the TCP handshake.
The request goes over the finished connection.

questions.stem: After one side of a TCP connection sends FIN and gets an ACK, the other side can still send data.

options.explanation: Correct: the connection is half-closed until the other side sends its own FIN.
It can: the connection is only half-closed at that point.

questions.stem: Which does UDP NOT guarantee? Select 3.

options.explanation: UDP has no guarantee of delivery.
Packets can arrive out of order.
There's no duplicate protection.
UDP does provide port numbers.

questions.stem: A live video call would rather lose a packet than wait for it to be resent. Which transport suits it?

options.explanation: Time-sensitive apps prefer dropping packets to waiting for retransmission.
TCP waits for lost data to be resent, adding delay.
HTTP is an application protocol that normally relies on TCP.
NAT shares addresses; it isn't a transport.

questions.stem: UDP sets up a connection with a handshake before sending data.

options.explanation: UDP has no handshaking dialogues.
Correct: UDP is connectionless.

questions.stem: Which statement about latency is right?

options.text: Low latency is good: little delay
options.explanation: Latency is delay, so less is better.

options.text: High latency means a faster connection
options.explanation: High latency means long waits.

options.text: Latency is how much data fits through a connection per second
options.explanation: That's bandwidth.

options.text: Latency only applies to video codecs
options.explanation: Network latency is the most common use of the term.

questions.stem: Which command measures round-trip time to a host?

options.explanation: ping sends packets and reports min/avg/max round-trip times.
whois looks up who registered a domain.
curl makes requests, it doesn't report RTT statistics.
kubectl talks to the Kubernetes API.

questions.stem: You create a Kubernetes Service and don't set `protocol` on its port. Which protocol does it use?

options.explanation: TCP is the default.
UDP must be set explicitly.
SCTP must be set explicitly and needs plugin support.
HTTP isn't a valid `protocol` value; it typically runs over TCP.

questions.stem: Which are valid values for a Service port's `protocol`? Select 3.

options.explanation: The default.
Valid; for LoadBalancer Services it depends on the cloud provider.
Valid with a supporting network plugin.
HTTPS is a special case over TCP, not a `protocol` value.
